guidelines_detail.benefit: It benefits blind and low vision users of assistive technologies by enabling compatibility with screen readers and may also benefit users with cognitive disabilities. Properly assigning roles or properties to status messages allows for possible future uses and personalization opportunities, while also providing additional information to users without affecting their current point of regard. Additionally, assistive technologies may choose to delay, suppress, or transform such messages based on the user’s preferences.
guidelines_detail.developer_action: The status message provides information to the user on the success or results of an action, on the waiting state of an application, on the progress of a process, or on the existence of errors; the message is not delivered via a change in context.
guidelines_detail.evaluator_action: The evaluator will test it manually and by using the Accessibility extension to browser/ Accessibility plug-in/Web Accessibility tool/ Assistive Technology to check the conformity of this checkpoint.

checkpoints.title: Pre-Production Security Audit Clearance (NIC / STQC / CERT-In)
checkpoints.requirement_text: The website, web application, web portal or mobile app is Security Audited and an Audit Clearance certificate is issued by NIC, STQC or a CERT-In empaneled vendor before hosting in production environment.
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Obscured Server/X-Powered-By version headers, defense-in-depth HTTP security headers, and optional public STQC/CQW badge.
checkpoints.caveats: Absence of a public badge does NOT prove lack of a Safe-to-Host certificate; internal code/DB security audits can only be verified via official STQC/CERT-In records. Never probe or actively scan government servers.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Check if the portal publicly discloses a STQC Certified Quality Website (CQW) / CERT-In Safe-to-Host badge or security audit date (optional public indicator); actual certificate validity, OWASP ASVS code review, DB encryption, and annual re-audit records are strictly internal.

guidelines_detail.benefit: The goal of securing a website, web application, web portal or mobile app is to maintain the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information and services. This goal is accomplished through the implementation of best security practices in design, development and deployment. Attacks could cause both personal embarrassment and financial risks.
guidelines_detail.government_organisation_action: It should be ensured that the website, web application, web portal or mobile app don’t have any security risks as identified by the latest OWASP Top 10 vulnerability list. The design and development agency or the developers should follow industry best practices such as OWASP ASVS and OWASP MAVS.
guidelines_detail.developer_action:
Securing critical web resources is more important than ever as the focus of attackers has steadily moved towards the application layer and they are exploiting the weaknesses in the code.
Securing Code:
Ensure that all Websites, Web Applications, Web Portals or Mobile Apps and their respective Content Management System (CMS), 3rd party plugins, codes, etc. are updated to the latest versions.
Note: Every day, there are countless websites compromised due to outdated software. Potential hackers and bots are scanning sites to attack. Updates are vital to the health and security of the website. If the site’s software or applications are not up-to-date, the site is not secure. Take all software and plugin update requests seriously. Updates often contain security enhancements and vulnerability repairs. Check the site for updates or add an update notification plugin. Some platforms allow automatic updates, which is another option to ensure website security. The longer you wait, the less secure the site will be. Updating the website and its components should be top priority.
All passwords, connection strings, tokens, keys, etc. should be encrypted with salted hash. There should not be any plain passwords stored in config files or source code or in a database.
All exceptions should be handled appropriately. Custom error pages should be displayed for any errors/exceptions. At no point of time, a portion of source code should be displayed on the page in case of an error or exception.
HTTP Response Headers should be obscured.
Cookies should be secure and HTTP only.
Configure captcha for login pages.
Directory traversal should be disabled. In case of any specific attempt by a user to access a portion of the code by typing the URL path (ex: www.xxx.gov.in/js/custom.js) then the same should be redirected to a custom error page.
All default user names and IIS/Apache pages (like admin, default.aspx, index.aspx, etc.) should be renamed. The access URL for the admin panel/CMS, should also be renamed.
The Web Server processes should not be running under Administrator or Root user Account. A dedicated User account with limited privileges should be used for the Web Server Processes.
Note: Not every webmaster knows which web server they use. If you are one of them, use a website scanner like SiteCheck to check the website. It scans for known malware, viruses, blacklisting status, website errors, and more. The more you know about the current state of website security, the better. It gives you time to fix it before any harm comes to it.
If the web or mobile app is integrated with any 3rd party Applications or using any APIs for external communication, then ensure that all such communications are done through encrypted channels.
Enforce strong password management policy, secure password recovery mechanisms and multi-factor authentication (MFA) for user login to website, web application or web portal infrastructure.
Implement role-based access control and minimal privilege policy for users as per need from the system.
Establish the secure coding practices document based on leading practices such as OWASP for code development. Below is an indicative checklist that can be considered for secure code development.
Input Validation
Authentication & Password Management
Session Management
Access Control
Cryptographic Practices
Error Handling & Logging
Data Protection
Communication Security
System Configuration
Database Security
File Management
Memory Management
Implement logging functionality and periodically auditing the web logs for suspicious activity.
Configure website, web application or web portal caching to optimize resource availability.
Sanitise user input at both the client end and the server end with both syntactical as well as a semantic approach.
The technology to be implemented should be chosen after careful consideration. Various client-side Active Content Technologies are available e.g., Java scripts etc. Each has its own strengths and weaknesses along with an associated risk.
Disable the root user access to run the code on Linux/Unix hosts.
Use explicit path names when invoking external programs and not rely on the PATH environment value.
Securing Databases: Database being the core of any application and/or organisation and is used to store large amounts of highly sensitive and personal information. Therefore, appropriate technical controls should be in place to safeguard the databases and information stored in them. The following are the guidelines for securing databases:
Implement strong encryption and key management mechanism for the information both at rest and transit.
Implement strong hashing and salting algorithms to store passwords in the database.
Use secure credentials for database access. Remove or change all default database administrative passwords.
Utilise strong passwords/phrases or implement multi-factor authentication.
Disable unnecessary accounts such as orphaned accounts, unused accounts, generic and service accounts.
Enable access to the database only from the Web Server on a whitelisted port and it should not be assigned publicly accessible IP.
TLS should be enabled in databases for secure communications between web servers and databases.
Create admin restrictions, such as by controlling privileged access on what users can do in a database.
The application should use the lowest possible level of privilege when accessing the database.
Turn on node checking to verify applications and users.
Turn off all unnecessary database functionality (e.g., unnecessary stored procedures or services, utility packages, install only the minimum set of features and options required (surface area reduction)
Enforce a strict access control policy and introduce role-based access control (RBAC) privileges.
Enable audit trail logs on the database servers.
Ensure appropriate logging and monitoring of database logs.
Consider fine grained record/row level auditing based on the sensitivity of data.
Implement a backup solution to store data and system configurations from the website, web application or web portal that should be backed up periodically.
Note: One of the best methods to keep a site safe is to have a good backup solution. You should have more than one. Each is crucial to recovering a website after a major security incident occurs. There are several different solutions you can use to help recover damaged or lost files. Keep the website information off-site. Do not store the backups on the same server as of the website; they are as vulnerable to attacks too. Choose to keep the website backup on a home computer or hard drive. Find an off-site place to store the data and to protect it from hardware failures, hacks, and viruses. Another option is to back up the website in the cloud. It makes storing data easy and allows access to information from anywhere. Besides choosing where to back up the website, you must consider automating them. Use a solution where you can schedule the site backups. You also have to ensure the solution has a reliable recovery system. Be redundant in the backup process — backup the backups. By doing this, you can recover files from any point before the hack or virus occurs.
Keep the backup media file in safe custody and access to it should be restricted and logged.
Conduct periodic auditing of Web Application – at least once in a year or as and when any changes are done in the source code, whichever is earlier.
Report any web application-related security incidents observed to NIC CERT & CERT-In immediately at Incident Response Help Desk:
NIC-CERT : incident[at]nic-cert[dot]nic[dot]in
CERT-In : incident[at]cert-in[dot]org[dot]in
Toll free phone : CERT-In – +91-1800-11-4949
guidelines_detail.evaluator_action: The evaluator shall check that the website/ web application/ web portal/ mobile app under evaluation has a valid security audit certificate issued by NIC/STQC/STQC empanelled laboratory/ Cert-IN empanelled laboratory fulfilling Cert-IN requirements.

checkpoints.title: Secured Hosting Environment (CIA, HTTPS/HSTS, TLS, Hardening, DC/DR)
checkpoints.requirement_text: Hosting Environment must be secured for ensuring confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA).
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Valid HTTPS/TLS certificate, HSTS header, and obscured server version banner.
checkpoints.caveats: Passive HTTPS/HSTS observation covers only the public transport layer of GIGW 5.3.2; hosting infrastructure CIA controls require backend HSP/STQC verification. Zero active port scanning or vulnerability probing is permitted.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Review observed passive TLS/HTTPS and HSTS results; data-centre India residency, DC/DR seismic separation, WAF deployment, 180-day CERT-In log retention, container hardening, and OS patching are internal hosting controls.

guidelines_detail.benefit: The goal of securing a hosting environment is to maintain the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information resources leading to successful operations. This goal is accomplished through the implementation of security controls. Hosting service providers should follow industry best practices for securing the hosting environment. Attacks could cause both personal embarrassment and financial risks. Secure hosting as well as doing regular backups save the time and money put into the site. Further having a contigency management plan helps the department manage the situation arising out of Defacement/ Natural Calamity
guidelines_detail.government_organisation_action:
Think of a website’s domain name as a street address. Now, think of the web host as the plot of “real estate” where the website exists online. As one would research a plot of land to build a house, it needs to examine potential web hosts to find the right one. Many hosts provide server security features that better protect a website and its data.
There are certain mandatory aspects to check for when choosing a hosting service provider (HSP):
Ensure the hosting of the web infrastructure within geographical boundaries of India.
Department to ensure the HSP is providing DC, BCP and DR environments with state-of-the-art secure infrastructure configured in high availability (HA) mode for hosting the Websites, Web Applications, Web Portals or Mobile Apps and their respective Content Management System (CMS). The HSP must ensure that the Primary Data Centre(DC), Disaster Recovery Center (DRC) are geographically located far from each other in different seismic zones. Further the department must have a contingency management plan to ensure availability in case of defacement and / or natural calamity.
Conduct periodic drills of disaster recovery environment – at least once in a year.
HSP to ensure that the servers are protected against environmental, physical and cyber threats.
Ensure the HSP has implemented all security controls of the Data Center including physical security and appropriate access control mechanisms.
Servers, Network devices used to host the website should be hardened with latest security patches and periodic Vulnerability Assessment (VA) and Penetration Testing (PT) followed by corrective actions should be performed as per the security policy.
Ensure the HSP of the hosting environment has deployed and configured a Web Application Firewall (WAF), which is hardened with latest security patches and is available for use by the department on demand.
Note: It sits between the website server and the data connection. The purpose is to read every bit of data that passes through it to protect the site. Most WAFs are cloud-based and are a plug-and-play service. The cloud service is a gateway to all incoming traffic that blocks all hacking attempts. It also filters out other types of unwanted traffic, like spammers and malicious bots.
Enable and maintain logs of the ICT infrastructure for a rolling period of 180 days as per CERT-In directions.
Regularly monitor and conduct review of alerts and logs
HSP should also ensure:
Web host offer a Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP)
FTP use by unknown users are disabled
It uses a rootkit scanner
HSP should ensure to secure the containerized environments, if applicable.
Note: Containerized Workloads are much more complex than traditional workloads. Production environments deploy massive amounts of containers. Security experts and administrators need to secure more components in a containerized environment than they would in traditional deployments. Container security involves the implementation and maintenance of security controls that protect containers and the underlying infrastructure. Integrating security into the development pipeline can help ensure that all components are secured from the initial development phase and until the end of their lifecycle.
Following best practices should be used to protect the containerized environments:
Each library and tool you pull into the image poses a potential threat. To mitigate these threats, you need to include the application within the container image. This should be a statically compiled binary that contains all required dependencies.
Remove all components the application does not need. For example, remove the “sed” and “awk” binaries, which are present by default on any UNIX system. This can help you reduce the attack surface.
If you are not creating the image from scratch, you should choose images that are trustworthy. Public image repositories, such as Docker Hub, can be used by anyone and may contain malware or misconfigurations.
If you have a private registry, you need to establish access controls that define exactly who can access and publish images and who cannot perform these actions.
Signatures help track images to the people who signed them. This makes it difficult to substitute the signed image for a compromised one. The Docker Content Trust mechanism provides information about signing images. You can also use Notary, an open-source tool that helps you sign and verify images.
Vulnerability scanners are designed to identify known vulnerabilities. These tools can help you find critical vulnerabilities and detect critical threats. You can use scanners on a continuous basis to ensure that the registries do not contain critical vulnerabilities.
Secure the target environment – You can do this by hardening the underlying host operating system. You can also establish firewall and VPC rules or create special accounts that limit access.
Use an orchestration platform – These systems usually provide secure API endpoints as well as role-based access control (RBAC), which can help minimise the risk of unauthorised access.
Use immutable deployments – This involves creating an instance image during the build steps. The deployment can then use this image to create new instances. To update the application, you need to create new images, spin up new instances, and then destroy the old ones.
Create separate virtual networks for the containers – This introduces a level of isolation that can reduce the attack surface.
Apply the principle of least privilege – Allow connectivity only between containers that truly need it.
Expose only the ports that serve the application – Do not expose any other ports, except for SSH. Apply this principle to containers as well as the underlying machines.
Use TLS to secure communication between services – This process encrypts traffic and ensures only authorised endpoints are allowed.
Use the Docker Image policy plugin – This plugin is designed to prevent any process from pulling images that were not previously allow-listed.
Enable TLS everywhere – You should enable TLS for all supported components to defend against traffic sniffing and authenticate identities at both ends of each connection.
Use a service mesh architecture – Service meshes are networks of persistent encrypted connections between high-performance sidecar proxies. They provide traffic monitoring, management, and policy enforcement without affecting microservices.
Use OPA – Open Policy Agent (OPA) enforces custom policies on a Kubernetes object without reconfiguring or recompiling the Kubernetes API server.
Apply network policies – The default Kubernetes networking permits all traffic between pods, but you can restrict this with a network policy.
Implement private networks – Deploy each Kubernetes worker and master node on a private subnet to secure the connections to corporate networks, make nodes unreachable from the public Internet, and minimise overall attack surface.
Keep the etcd cluster separate – Use a firewall to protect the etcd cluster, which stores state and secret information and requires special protection compared to other Kubernetes components.
Ensure the regular rotation of encryption keys – Regularly rotating encryption keys and certificates helps minimise the blast radius of an attack that compromises keys.
Use static analysis for YAML – Statically analyse where pod security policies deny access to API servers. This should be part of the development workflow because it helps identify the organisation’s risk tolerance and compliance requirements.
Manage secrets – Integrate clusters using a secret management system to ensure application pods automatically receive all secrets and passwords needed at runtime (based on the app roles associated with each pod).
Check the code – Scan the code and use static analysis to ensure automation security. You must scan the source code for all application code in Kubernetes to identify vulnerabilities and hard-coded errors.
Use RBAC policies based on the principle of least privilege – Role-based access control (RBAC) helps manage access policies at a granular level to protect resources. A centralised authentication and authorization system like SSO throughout the organisation makes onboarding and offboarding easier.
WIM must mention in security policy if website under thier control should be accessible outside india or not. If the same is required, then they may clarify that in which countries the website may be made accessible (or accessible everywhere). This mechanism will mitigate the risk of external cyber attacks and the same will protect the web applications from data breaches and other threats. Accordingly, firewall rules for the websites may be configured.
guidelines_detail.developer_action:
Following activities are to be ensured by the Developer i.e., in this case it’s System Admin or DevOps:
Restrict the admin access and implement the principle of least privilege and disable unnecessary accounts and privileges.
Disable all unnecessary ports opened on the web server i.e., deny all access by default.
Remove default, temporary or guest accounts from the web server.
Change the default login credentials and implement strong password enforcement with password expiration policy on the web server.
Note: With there being so many websites, databases, and programs needing passwords, it is hard to keep track. A lot of people end up using the same password in all places, to remember their login information. But this is a significant security mistake. Create a unique password for every new login request. Come up with complicated, random, and difficult to guess passwords. Then, store them outside the website directory. For example, you might use a 14-digit mixture of letters and numbers as a password. You could then store the password(s) in an offline file, a smartphone, or a different computer. When CMS requests to login you must choose a smart password. Refrain from using any personal information inside the password. Do not use birthday or pet’s name; make it completely unguessable. After three months or sooner, change the password to another one, then repeat. Smart passwords are long and should be at least twelve characters, every time. A password needs to be a combination of numbers and symbols. Make sure to alternate between uppercase and lowercase letters. Never use the same password twice or share it with others. If you are a business owner or CMS manager, ensure all employees change their passwords frequently.
Whitelist the application in use and disable the unused features or modules.
Use of Secure FTP (SFTP) to transfer files over an encrypted channel.
Disable Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and enforce Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) & HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS). To keep a website safe, it needs a secure URL. If a user uses their private information to access a site, it should use HTTPS, not HTTP, to deliver it.
Note: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) is a protocol used to provide security over the Internet. HTTPS prevents interceptions and interruptions from occurring while the content is in transit. For you to create a secure online connection, a website also needs an SSL Certificate. If the website asks visitors to register, sign-up, or make a transaction of any kind, you need to encrypt the connection. SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is another necessary site protocol. This transfers visitor’s personal information between the website and the database. SSL encrypts information to prevent it from others reading it while in transit. It denies those without proper authority the ability to access the data, as well. GlobalSign is an example of an SSL certificate that works with most websites.
Mandatorily use a valid SSL Certificate on all websites. The SSL Certificate should use at least 2048-bit SHA 256 encryption or higher.
Ensure that the SSL Certificate is valid and keep track of the certificate expiry date and take necessary action to renew/replace the certificate before expiry.
Configure the HTTP Service banner so that Web Server and Operating System type & version will not be disclosed.
The configuration files of the Web Server must be protected by the Web Server process. One can find them in the root web directory. Web server configuration files permit you to administer server rules. This includes directives to improve website security. There are different file types used with every server. Learn about the one you use.
Apache web servers use the .htaccess file
Nginx servers use nginx.conf
Microsoft IIS servers use web.config
Open source/Freeware software should be used with due diligence.
Remove or disable all superfluous drivers, services and software.
Remove or replace obsolete software libraries.
Remove or replace outdated security level protocols.
Limit unauthorised or unauthenticated or administrative privilege user access to the system.
Note: Initially, one may feel comfortable giving several high-level employees access to a website. Administrative privileges are given thinking those would be used carefully. Although this is the ideal situation, it is not always the case. Unfortunately, employees do not think about website security when logging into the Servers or the CMS. Instead, their thoughts are on the task at hand. If they make a mistake or overlook an issue, this can result in a significant security issue. It is vital to access employees before giving website access. Find out if they have experience using the CMS and if they know what to look for to avoid a security breach. Educate every CMS user about the importance of passwords and software updates. Tell them all the ways they can help maintain the website’s safety. To keep track of who has access to CMS and their administrative settings, make a record and update it often. Employees come and go. One of the best ways to prevent security issues is to have a physical record of who does what with the website. Be sensible when it comes to user access.
Implement encryption for the transmission of all sensitive information. This should include TLS for protecting the connection. Disable weak cyphers (SSLv2, SSlv3, 3DES, RC4, TLS v1.0, v1.1).
Periodically review logs for suspicious activity like authentication, user access activity & changes and privilege elevation & usage.
Implementation of network segmentation and segregation to limit the impact of network intrusion.
There should be no active concurrent sessions of the web server.
Ensure servers, frameworks and system components are running the latest approved version and have all patches issued for the version in use.
Isolate development environments from the production network and provide access only to authorised development and test groups.
Implement a software change control system to manage and record changes to the code both in development and production.
Establish practice of hardening web servers and conduct the periodic secure configuration review of the same.
The most common attacks against websites are entirely automated. What many attack bots rely on is for users to have their CMS settings on default. After choosing a CMS, change default settings immediately. Changes help prevent a large number of attacks from occurring. CMS settings can include adjusting control comments, user visibility, and permissions. A great example of a default setting change you should make is ‘file permissions.’ You can change the permissions to specify who can do what to a file. Each file has three permissions and a number that represents every permission:
‘Read‘ (4): View the file contents.
‘Write‘ (2): Change the file contents.
‘Execute‘ (1): Run the program file or script.
To clarify, if you want to allow many permissions, add the numbers together. E.g., to allow read (4) and write (2), you set the user permission to (6.) Along with the default file permission settings, there are three user types:
Owner – Often, the creator of the file, but ownership can be changed. Only one user can be the owner at a time.
Group – Each file is assigned to a group. Users who are part of that specific group will gain access to the permissions of the group.
Public – Everyone else.
Customise users and their permission settings. Do not keep the default settings as is, or you will run into website security issues at some point.

checkpoints.caveats: Subject to 'within a reasonable time and subject to availability of resources'. checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Only assessable via internal records audit or official public authority statement on record management/digitisation. Partial/stale: Not determinable from public web pages alone.

checkpoints.title: Budget Allocated, Plans, Proposed Expenditures and Disbursement Reports
checkpoints.requirement_text: Proactively publish budget allocations (BE/RE) across agencies/schemes, proposed expenditures/plans, and reports on actual disbursements/expenditure.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(1)(b)(xi)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Link to Budget / Demand for Grants / Expenditure / Outcome Budget / Annual Report or RTI Manual-11.
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Authority-specific budget allocations, proposed plan/scheme outlays, and actual expenditure/disbursement reports for recent fiscal year(s). Partial/stale: Shows only high-level allocation without disbursement/actual expenditure, or latest published budget is >2 financial years old.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (xi) the budget allocated to each of its agency, indicating the particulars of all plans, proposed expenditures and reports on disbursements made;
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — Budget, Plans & Annual Reports

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Authority-specific budget allocations, proposed plan/scheme outlays, and actual expenditure/disbursement reports for recent fiscal year(s).
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Shows only high-level allocation without disbursement/actual expenditure, or latest published budget is >2 financial years old.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No agency-level budget, expenditure, or disbursement report observed.
benign_explanations: Field units whose budget is pooled inside a parent ministry's Demand for Grants may reference the parent ministry's budget page.

checkpoints.title: Manner of Execution of Subsidy Programmes, Allocations and Beneficiaries
checkpoints.requirement_text: Proactively publish how subsidy/welfare programmes are executed, criteria, amounts allocated, and summary/programme-level beneficiary disclosures (or explicitly state if no subsidy programme is operated).
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(1)(b)(xii)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Section 4(1)(b)(xii) / Manual-12 disclosure or Schemes/Subsidies/DBT dashboard link.
checkpoints.caveats: Regulatory/administrative authorities that operate no subsidy schemes satisfy this clause by explicitly stating 'Not Applicable / Nil'. Note RTI Sec 8(1)(j) as amended by DPDP Act 2023 w.e.f. 13-11-2025 limits personal data publication. Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Publishes subsidy execution guidelines, allocated amounts, and beneficiary reporting/dashboard (or explicitly states Nil/N/A where no subsidy exists). Partial/stale: Describes scheme eligibility qualitatively but omits budget allocations or disbursement/beneficiary summaries.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (xii) the manner of execution of subsidy programmes, including the amounts allocated and the details of beneficiaries of such programmes;
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — Schemes & Programmes

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Publishes subsidy execution guidelines, allocated amounts, and beneficiary reporting/dashboard (or explicitly states Nil/N/A where no subsidy exists).
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Describes scheme eligibility qualitatively but omits budget allocations or disbursement/beneficiary summaries.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: Neither subsidy programme disclosure nor an explicit 'Not Applicable' statement observed on RTI pages.
benign_explanations: Public authority may not operate any subsidy programme, or beneficiary dashboards may be hosted on dbtbharat.gov.in.

checkpoints.title: Particulars of Recipients of Concessions, Permits or Authorisations Granted
checkpoints.requirement_text: Proactively publish particulars/registers of entities granted concessions, licences, permits, or authorisations (or explicitly state if none are granted).
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(1)(b)(xiii)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Section 4(1)(b)(xiii) / Manual-13 statement or public register of licences/permits/concessions.
checkpoints.caveats: Authorities that do not grant concessions/permits/licences satisfy this clause by stating 'Not Applicable / Nil'. Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Publishes public register/list of institutional recipients of concessions/permits/authorisations, or explicitly states Nil/N/A. Partial/stale: Describes how to apply for a permit but publishes no register or historical list of granted permits/concessions.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (xiii) particulars of recipients of concessions, permits or authorisations granted by it;
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — RTI Proactive Disclosure

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Publishes public register/list of institutional recipients of concessions/permits/authorisations, or explicitly states Nil/N/A.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Describes how to apply for a permit but publishes no register or historical list of granted permits/concessions.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: Neither concession/permit recipient disclosure nor an explicit N/A statement observed.
benign_explanations: Authority may not issue permits/concessions, or licensing registries may reside on a dedicated regulatory portal (e.g., Parivesh/NSWS).

checkpoints.title: Details of Information Available or Held in Electronic Form
checkpoints.requirement_text: Proactively publish an index/inventory detailing what information, databases, manuals, and records have been reduced to electronic form and where they can be accessed.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(1)(b)(xiv)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Section 4(1)(b)(xiv) / Manual-14 inventory listing digitised datasets, web portals, and electronic publications.
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Itemised inventory of databases, reports, manuals, and portals available in electronic form with access pointers. Partial/stale: Generic one-liner stating 'Most information is on the website' without listing electronic holdings.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (xiv) details in respect of the information, available to or held by it, reduced in an electronic form;
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Sitemap & Electronic Document Catalogues

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Itemised inventory of databases, reports, manuals, and portals available in electronic form with access pointers.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Generic one-liner stating 'Most information is on the website' without listing electronic holdings.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No Section 4(1)(b)(xiv) electronic-form information inventory observed.
benign_explanations: Details may be listed inside a site map or consolidated Section 4(1)(b) PDF manual.

checkpoints.title: Facilities Available to Citizens for Obtaining Information (incl. Library/Reading Room Hours)
checkpoints.requirement_text: Proactively publish citizen access facilities — information/facilitation counters, office hours, public library/reading room timings (if maintained), notice boards, and online portals.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(1)(b)(xv)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Section 4(1)(b)(xv) / Manual-15 block detailing facilitation counter, office timings, library/reading room status, and web access.
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Specifies citizen access mechanisms (website, facilitation counter/reception, office timings, inspection procedure, and library/reading room status). Partial/stale: Mentions only the website URL without office timings, facilitation counter, or physical inspection details.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (xv) the particulars of facilities available to citizens for obtaining information, including the working hours of a library or reading room, if maintained for public use;
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Quality Checkpoint 10 & 14 (Contact Us / Help / Citizen Facilities)

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Specifies citizen access mechanisms (website, facilitation counter/reception, office timings, inspection procedure, and library/reading room status).
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Mentions only the website URL without office timings, facilitation counter, or physical inspection details.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No Section 4(1)(b)(xv) citizen information facilities disclosure observed.
benign_explanations: Details may be integrated into a Contact Us or Citizen's Charter page rather than a separate RTI table.

checkpoints.title: Names, Designations and Other Particulars of Public Information Officers
checkpoints.requirement_text: Proactively publish the names, official designations, subject-matter jurisdiction, office addresses, and official contact channels of all designated CPIOs / SPIOs.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(1)(b)(xvi)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Explicit CPIO / SPIO / Public Information Officer designation text or dedicated PIO directory link on homepage, Contact page, or RTI page.
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Published list/table naming current CPIO/SPIO designation(s) and official contact channel(s) on RTI or Contact page. Partial/stale: Mentions 'CPIO' generically without officer designation/office details or lists visibly retired/outdated officeholders.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (xvi) the names, designations and other particulars of the Public Information Officers;
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — RTI / Contact Us (PIO Details)

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Published list/table naming current CPIO/SPIO designation(s) and official contact channel(s) on RTI or Contact page.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Mentions 'CPIO' generically without officer designation/office details or lists visibly retired/outdated officeholders.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No CPIO/SPIO/Public Information Officer designation or listing observed on sampled pages.
benign_explanations: PIO list may be inside an embedded PDF or hosted on a parent ministry/state RTI portal.

checkpoints.title: Such Other Information as May Be Prescribed
checkpoints.requirement_text: Proactively publish any additional categories prescribed by rules or DoPT/State Government Section 4 suo motu directives (e.g., annual reports, transparency audit reports, FAQs, RTI disposal stats).
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(1)(b)(xvii)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Section 4(1)(b)(xvii) / Manual-17 heading linking annual reports, FAQs, parliamentary Q&A, or DoPT prescribed items.
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Addresses item (xvii) with prescribed/additional transparency disclosures (e.g., annual report, FAQs, RTI statistics, audit reports). Partial/stale: Heading present with blank cell or 'To be updated' placeholder.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (xvii) such other information as may be prescribed;
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — RTI / DoPT Prescribed Proactive Disclosures

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Addresses item (xvii) with prescribed/additional transparency disclosures (e.g., annual report, FAQs, RTI statistics, audit reports).
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Heading present with blank cell or 'To be updated' placeholder.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: Section 4(1)(b)(xvii) not addressed on RTI proactive disclosure page.
benign_explanations: Additional disclosures may be spread across homepage sections (Annual Reports, Tenders, Parliament Questions) without an explicit Manual-17 label.

checkpoints.title: Annual Updating of All 17 Section 4(1)(b) Proactive Disclosures
checkpoints.requirement_text: Every public authority must review and update its 17 Section 4(1)(b) proactive disclosure publications at least once every year, with visible update currency.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(1)(b) (Concluding Mandate)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Last Updated / Reviewed date on the RTI proactive disclosure page itself (distinct from homepage footer auto-timestamp) and fiscal year currency inside tables.
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: RTI Section 4(1)(b) disclosures show clear revision/data currency within the last 12–18 months (current or preceding fiscal year). Partial/stale: RTI manual exists but dates/budgets/officer lists are visibly >2 years stale (e.g., last revised 2018-2022).
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: and thereafter update these publications every year;
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Quality Checkpoint 5 (Last Updated / Reviewed Date & Content Review Policy)

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: RTI Section 4(1)(b) disclosures show clear revision/data currency within the last 12–18 months (current or preceding fiscal year).
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: RTI manual exists but dates/budgets/officer lists are visibly >2 years stale (e.g., last revised 2018-2022).
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No revision date or fiscal-year currency indicator observed on RTI proactive disclosure pages.
benign_explanations: Static HTML manuals sometimes omit an explicit 'updated on' line even after silent content edits; check internal fiscal-year references.

checkpoints.title: Publishing Relevant Facts While Formulating Policies or Announcing Public Decisions
checkpoints.requirement_text: Proactively publish background facts, policy drafts, notifications, circulars, and explanatory materials when formulating important policies or announcing decisions affecting the public.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(1)(c)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Presence of Policy Documents / Notifications / Press Releases / Public Notices section with explanatory background notes.
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Publishes policy papers, notifications, background notes, or explanatory announcements for major public-facing decisions. Partial/stale: Publishes terse order numbers without explanatory background facts or stops updating policy notices.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (c) publish all relevant facts while formulating important policies or announcing the decisions which affect public;
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — What's New, Press Releases & Policy Documents

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Publishes policy papers, notifications, background notes, or explanatory announcements for major public-facing decisions.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Publishes terse order numbers without explanatory background facts or stops updating policy notices.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No policy facts, public notices, or decision announcements section observed.
benign_explanations: Purely technical/support offices that do not formulate public policy may have minimal policy announcements.

checkpoints.title: Providing Reasons for Administrative or Quasi-Judicial Decisions to Affected Persons
checkpoints.requirement_text: Public authorities must communicate reasons for administrative or quasi-judicial decisions to affected persons (with quasi-judicial tribunals/regulators often also publishing reasoned orders online).
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(1)(d)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Optional positive indicator on tribunal/regulator portals: public Orders/Judgments archive.
checkpoints.caveats: Primarily an individual-decision obligation owed directly to affected persons; public web publication of reasoned orders is common for tribunals/regulators but not universally required on websites for routine administrative files. Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Requires case-file inspection or review of orders communicated to affected parties; only web-observable on tribunals/regulators that publish orders online. Partial/stale: Not determinable solely from general department homepages.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (d) provide reasons for its administrative or quasi-judicial decisions to affected persons.
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: N/A — Statutory Administrative/Quasi-Judicial Process Obligation

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Requires case-file inspection or review of orders communicated to affected parties; only web-observable on tribunals/regulators that publish orders online.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Not determinable solely from general department homepages.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: Classify as internal_governance / unassessable via public HTML crawl.
benign_explanations: Reasons for individual administrative decisions are delivered directly to affected persons and may contain personal data exempt under Section 8(1)(j).

checkpoints.title: Suo Motu Proactive Disclosure via Internet (Dedicated RTI / Suo Motu Navigation)
checkpoints.requirement_text: Public authorities must continuously publish suo motu information on the internet through a clear, discoverable RTI / Right to Information / Suo Motu Disclosure section so citizens have minimum need to file formal RTI applications.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(2)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Visible <a> navigation/header/footer link on homepage matching RTI / Right to Information / Suo Motu Disclosure / Section 4(1)(b) (same-origin page or parent authority RTI page).
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Dedicated, visible RTI / Right to Information / Proactive Disclosure link present on homepage leading to reachable RTI disclosures. Partial/stale: RTI link exists on homepage but points only to a PDF copy of the bare RTI Act 2005 without the authority's own disclosures, or leads to 404.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (2) It shall be a constant endeavour of every public authority to take steps in accordance with the requirements of clause (b) of sub-section (1) to provide as much information suomotu to the public at regular intervals through various means of communications, including internet, so that the public have minimum resort to the use of this Act to obtain information.
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — Mandatory RTI / Proactive Disclosure Section

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Dedicated, visible RTI / Right to Information / Proactive Disclosure link present on homepage leading to reachable RTI disclosures.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: RTI link exists on homepage but points only to a PDF copy of the bare RTI Act 2005 without the authority's own disclosures, or leads to 404.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No RTI / Right to Information / Suo Motu Disclosure link observed on landing page.
benign_explanations: Subdomain may be a single-function utility/API/dashboard whose parent department homepage hosts the RTI section.
Label may appear in an unhandled regional script or an image without alt text.

checkpoints.title: Wide Dissemination in Easily Accessible Form and Manner (incl. Internet)
checkpoints.requirement_text: Proactive disclosures must be organised and published on the web in a form and manner easily accessible to the public (not buried behind logins, broken links, or unreadable scans).
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(3) & Explanation
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: RTI page loads publicly over HTTPS without login wall, uses structured headings/tables or readable links, and avoids dead links.
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: RTI disclosures are reachable without login, clearly structured by Section 4(1)(b) items, and readable without broken links. Partial/stale: RTI page exists but key documents return 404/broken links, require login, or are unindexed bulk image scans.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (3) For the purposes of sub-section (1), every information shall be disseminated widely and in such form and manner which is easily accessible to the public. Explanation.—For the purposes of sub-sections (3) and (4), 'disseminated' means making known or communicated the information to the public through notice boards, newspapers, public announcements, media broadcasts, the internet or any other means, including inspection of offices of any public authority.
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Usability, Navigation & Accessibility Guidelines

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: RTI disclosures are reachable without login, clearly structured by Section 4(1)(b) items, and readable without broken links.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: RTI page exists but key documents return 404/broken links, require login, or are unindexed bulk image scans.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No easily accessible public RTI disclosure page observed.
benign_explanations: Transient server errors or strict robots.txt/WAF rules may prevent automated sampling (mark unassessable).

checkpoints.title: Dissemination in Local Language and Electronic Format (Free / Prescribed Cost)
checkpoints.requirement_text: Disseminated information should consider the local language of the area and be easily accessible in electronic format (HTML/accessible PDFs) free of charge online or at prescribed print/medium cost.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 4(4) & Explanation
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Presence of language switcher link/select element, <html lang='hi'|regional>, or native-script content alongside electronic HTML/PDF disclosures.
checkpoints.caveats: Local language depends on jurisdiction (Hindi/English for Union portals; respective State official language(s) + English for State/District portals). Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Portal provides content or a working language toggle in Hindi or the relevant regional/local language, with disclosures in electronic format. Partial/stale: Language toggle exists on homepage but RTI disclosures are only in English or toggle leads to empty/untranslated pages.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (4) All materials shall be disseminated taking into consideration the cost effectiveness, local language and the most effective method of communication in that local area and the information should be easily accessible, to the extent possible in electronic format with the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, available free or at such cost of the medium or the print cost price as may be prescribed.
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Quality & Multilingual Content Guidelines (Hindi / Regional Languages)

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Portal provides content or a working language toggle in Hindi or the relevant regional/local language, with disclosures in electronic format.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Language toggle exists on homepage but RTI disclosures are only in English or toggle leads to empty/untranslated pages.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: Only English observed with no Hindi/local language indicator on sampled pages.
benign_explanations: Specialised scientific/technical or national English-language portals may offer translation widgets rendered client-side via JS.

checkpoints.title: Designation and Public Listing of CPIO / SPIO Across Administrative Units
checkpoints.requirement_text: Public authorities must designate CPIOs (Union/UT) or SPIOs (State) across all administrative units and make their designations/particulars publicly discoverable (read with Section 4(1)(b)(xvi)).
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 5(1)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Visible CPIO / SPIO / PIO listing on RTI or Contact page.
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: CPIO/SPIO designations for administrative units/divisions are published clearly on the website. Partial/stale: Only one generic Nodal CPIO listed for a large multi-unit ministry without unit-wise CPIOs, or entries are outdated.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: Every public authority shall, within one hundred days of the enactment of this Act, designate as many officers as the Central Public Information Officers or State Public Information Officers, as the case may be, in all administrative units or offices under it as may be necessary to provide information to persons requesting for the information under this Act.
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — RTI / Public Information Officers

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: CPIO/SPIO designations for administrative units/divisions are published clearly on the website.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Only one generic Nodal CPIO listed for a large multi-unit ministry without unit-wise CPIOs, or entries are outdated.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No CPIO/SPIO designation observed on sampled pages.
benign_explanations: Subordinate unit CPIOs may be listed in a consolidated directory hosted on the parent ministry/state portal.

checkpoints.title: Designation and Public Listing of CAPIO / SAPIO at Sub-Divisional / Sub-District Level
checkpoints.requirement_text: Public authorities with sub-divisional or sub-district offices must designate CAPIOs / SAPIOs to receive and forward RTI applications and appeals, and list them publicly.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 5(2)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Visible CAPIO / SAPIO / APIO / Assistant Public Information Officer mention or table on RTI page.
checkpoints.caveats: Applies specifically to authorities having sub-divisional/sub-district or field-level units; single-headquarters bodies with no field offices may legitimately have no CAPIO/SAPIO. Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: CAPIO/SAPIO designations published (or authority explicitly clarifies single-unit structure with direct CPIO/SPIO). Partial/stale: Mentions CAPIO heading without listing regional/sub-divisional officers where authority has wide field presence.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (2) Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (1), every public authority shall designate an officer, within one hundred days of the enactment of this Act, at each sub-divisional level or other sub-district level as a Central Assistant Public Information Officer or a State Assistant Public Information Officer, as the case may be, to receive the applications for information or appeals under this Act for forwarding the same forthwith...
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — RTI Officers Directory

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: CAPIO/SAPIO designations published (or authority explicitly clarifies single-unit structure with direct CPIO/SPIO).
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Mentions CAPIO heading without listing regional/sub-divisional officers where authority has wide field presence.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No CAPIO/SAPIO designation observed on sampled pages.
benign_explanations: Headquarters-only agencies without sub-divisional/sub-district offices are not required to appoint CAPIOs/SAPIOs.

checkpoints.title: Electronic / Online RTI Application Channel and Filing Guidance
checkpoints.requirement_text: Provide citizens clear guidance and/or a link to the official online RTI filing portal (e.g., rtionline.gov.in for Union authorities or the applicable State RTI online portal) and prescribed filing procedure/fee modes.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 6(1)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Outbound link to rtionline.gov.in or state RTI online portal (e.g., rtionline.<state>.gov.in), or published RTI application filing instructions.
checkpoints.caveats: Central authorities route via https://rtionline.gov.in; State authorities MUST route to their respective State RTI portal or SPIO postal channel (NEVER rtionline.gov.in, which returns state requests without refund). Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Website links to the jurisdiction-appropriate online RTI portal and/or clearly explains how to submit an RTI request electronically or in writing. Partial/stale: Links to wrong jurisdiction portal (e.g., State authority linking to central rtionline.gov.in) or broken portal URL.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: A person, who desires to obtain any information under this Act, shall make a request in writing or through electronic means in English or Hindi or in the official language of the area in which the application is being made, accompanying such fee as may be prescribed...
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Online Services & RTI Citizen Interface

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Website links to the jurisdiction-appropriate online RTI portal and/or clearly explains how to submit an RTI request electronically or in writing.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Links to wrong jurisdiction portal (e.g., State authority linking to central rtionline.gov.in) or broken portal URL.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No online RTI portal link or RTI request filing procedure observed.
benign_explanations: Some States/UTs do not yet operate a centralised online RTI portal and accept electronic/postal applications directly via SPIO.

checkpoints.title: Assistance to Sensorily Disabled Citizens for Access to Records
checkpoints.requirement_text: CPIOs/SPIOs must provide reasonable assistance to sensorily disabled persons seeking access to or inspection of records.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 7(4)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Web accessibility itself is audited deterministically under RPwD Rule 15 (RPWD-15-1-c-i & RPWD-15-1-c-iii).
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Requires operational/request-level evaluation; web accessibility complements this under RPwD Rule 15. Partial/stale: Not determinable from public web pages alone.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (4) Where access to the record or a part thereof is required to be provided under this Act and the person to whom access is to be provided is sensorily disabled, the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, shall provide assistance to enable access to the information, including providing such assistance as may be appropriate for the inspection.
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Accessibility & RPwD Rules 2017 Rule 15

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Requires operational/request-level evaluation; web accessibility complements this under RPwD Rule 15.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Not determinable from public web pages alone.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: Classify as internal_governance.
benign_explanations: Statutory assistance under Section 7(4) occurs when processing individual requests or physical inspections.

checkpoints.title: Disclosure of Prescribed RTI Fee Rules and BPL Fee Exemption
checkpoints.requirement_text: RTI information pages should accurately state prescribed application/copying fees (and payment modes) along with the statutory exemption for Below Poverty Line (BPL) applicants.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 7(5) & Proviso
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Fee schedule and BPL exemption notice on the authority's RTI page.
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: RTI page states applicable application/reproduction fee, payment modes, and explicitly mentions BPL fee exemption. Partial/stale: Mentions Rs. 10 application fee but omits BPL exemption or copying cost schedule.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (5) Where access to information is to be provided in the printed or in any electronic format, the applicant shall, subject to the provisions of sub-section (6), pay such fee as may be prescribed: Provided that the fee prescribed under sub-section (1) of section 6 and sub-sections (1) and (5) of section 7 shall be reasonable and no such fee shall be charged from the persons who are of below poverty line as may be determined by the appropriate Government.
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — RTI Application & Fee Information

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: RTI page states applicable application/reproduction fee, payment modes, and explicitly mentions BPL fee exemption.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Mentions Rs. 10 application fee but omits BPL exemption or copying cost schedule.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No RTI fee or BPL exemption information observed on RTI pages.
benign_explanations: Authorities linking directly to rtionline.gov.in or a State RTI portal may rely on the central portal's fee instructions.

checkpoints.title: Public Disclosure of Completed Cabinet / Council of Ministers Decisions
checkpoints.requirement_text: Cabinet Secretariat, State General Administration Departments, and Ministries announcing completed Cabinet decisions must publish decisions, reasons, and non-exempt basis material once complete.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 8(1)(i) First Proviso
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Cabinet Decisions / Monthly Summary for Cabinet archive on Cabinet Secretariat or Ministry websites.
checkpoints.caveats: Second Proviso excludes matters falling under other Section 8(1) exemptions. Applies ONLY to Cabinet Secretariat, Chief Minister/Council of Ministers secretariats, and Union/State Ministries — NOT applicable to subordinate offices, courts, or autonomous institutes.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Cabinet Secretariat / Ministry / State GAD publishes completed Cabinet decisions and non-exempt summaries/reasons. Partial/stale: Publishes brief press headlines without decision summaries or archive is >1 year stale.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: Provided that the decisions of Council of Ministers, the reasons thereof, and the material on the basis of which the decisions were taken shall be made public after the decision has been taken, and the matter is complete, or over:
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — Decisions & Press Releases

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Cabinet Secretariat / Ministry / State GAD publishes completed Cabinet decisions and non-exempt summaries/reasons.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Publishes brief press headlines without decision summaries or archive is >1 year stale.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No completed Cabinet decision summaries observed on an applicable Cabinet/Ministry portal.
benign_explanations: Decisions may be published via Press Information Bureau (pib.gov.in) rather than duplicated on every ministry site.

checkpoints.title: Designation and Public Particulars of First Appellate Authority (FAA)
checkpoints.requirement_text: Publish the designation, senior rank, and official particulars of the First Appellate Authority (FAA) so citizens know where to file a Section 19(1) first appeal within 30 days.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 19(1)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Explicit 'First Appellate Authority' / 'Appellate Authority' listing alongside CPIO/SPIO on RTI or Contact page.
checkpoints.caveats: Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: First Appellate Authority designation (senior in rank to CPIO/SPIO) and official contact channel published on RTI/Contact page. Partial/stale: Mentions appeal right in abstract without identifying who the First Appellate Authority is.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: Any person who, does not receive a decision within the time specified in sub-section (1) or clause (a) of sub-section (3) of section 7, or is aggrieved by a decision of the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer, as the case may be, may within thirty days from the expiry of such period or from the receipt of such a decision prefer an appeal to such officer who is senior in rank to the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer as the case may be, in each public authority:
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — RTI & Appeal Mechanism

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: First Appellate Authority designation (senior in rank to CPIO/SPIO) and official contact channel published on RTI/Contact page.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Mentions appeal right in abstract without identifying who the First Appellate Authority is.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No First Appellate Authority designation or particulars observed on sampled pages.
benign_explanations: FAA details may reside inside a linked PIO/FAA PDF directory or on the parent authority's RTI page.

checkpoints.title: Annual RTI Implementation, Requests, Rejections and Appeals Reporting
checkpoints.requirement_text: Ministries/Departments must collect and furnish annual RTI statistics (requests, rejections by exemption clause, appeals, fees collected, disciplinary actions) to CIC/SIC and ideally publish quarterly/annual RTI returns or Annual Reports on their website.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 25(2) & Section 25(3)(a)-(g)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Quarterly/Annual RTI Returns table or Annual Report chapter reporting RTI receipts/disposals/rejections.
checkpoints.caveats: Statutory submission is made to CIC/SIC (which tables the consolidated report in Parliament/Legislature under Sec 25(4)); online publication of quarterly/annual RTI returns on the authority's own website is reinforced by DoPT OM 1/6/2011-IR. Does not apply to intelligence and security organisations specified in the Second Schedule (Section 24(1)) or State-notified intelligence/security organisations (Section 24(4)), except for specific statutory provisos. Single-purpose web apps/subdomains may satisfy web discoverability by linking prominently to their parent public authority's Section 4 disclosure portal.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Published annual/quarterly RTI disposal statistics (requests received, disposed, rejected, appeals) on RTI page or in Annual Report. Partial/stale: Only old RTI statistics (>2 years old) or aggregate counts without rejection/appeal breakdown.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (2) Each Ministry or Department shall, in relation to the public authorities within their jurisdiction, collect and provide such information to the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission, as the case may be, as is required to prepare the report under this section... (3) Each report shall state... (a) the number of requests made... (b) the number of decisions where applicants were not entitled... (c) the number of appeals... (d) particulars of any disciplinary action... (e) the amount of charges collected...
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: GIGW Content Guidelines — Annual Reports & RTI Disclosures

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Published annual/quarterly RTI disposal statistics (requests received, disposed, rejected, appeals) on RTI page or in Annual Report.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Only old RTI statistics (>2 years old) or aggregate counts without rejection/appeal breakdown.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: No public RTI annual/quarterly statistics observed on sampled pages.
benign_explanations: Authority may submit quarterly returns directly to the CIC/SIC Annual Report portal without mirroring them on its own site.

checkpoints.title: Appropriate Government RTI Educational Programmes and Official Training
checkpoints.requirement_text: Central and State Governments are encouraged to run citizen RTI awareness programmes and train CPIOs/SPIOs subject to resource availability.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 26(1)(a)-(d)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: N/A — Internal government capacity-building programme.
checkpoints.caveats: Discretionary ('may, to the extent of availability of financial and other resources') and addressed to the Appropriate Government (DoPT / State Administrative Reforms Departments), not individual subordinate websites.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Assessed at Appropriate Government (DoPT / State nodal RTI department / ATI) level via official programme reports. Partial/stale: Not determinable from individual department homepages.
checkpoints.statutory_text_excerpt: (1) The appropriate Government may, to the extent of availability of financial and other resources,— (a) develop and organise educational programmes to advance the understanding of the public, in particular of disadvantaged communities as to how to exercise the rights contemplated under this Act; ... (d) train Central Public Information Officers or State Public Information Officers...
checkpoints.gigw_cross_reference: N/A — Appropriate Government Programme Mandate

agent_inspection_rubric.observed_criteria: Assessed at Appropriate Government (DoPT / State nodal RTI department / ATI) level via official programme reports.
agent_inspection_rubric.partial_or_stale_criteria: Not determinable from individual department homepages.
agent_inspection_rubric.not_observed_criteria: Classify as internal_governance.
benign_explanations: Obligation rests on the Appropriate Government (Central/State), not individual line offices.

checkpoints.title: Appropriate Government Official-Language Citizen RTI Guide and Updated CPIO Directory
checkpoints.requirement_text: Central and State Governments must compile, publish, and periodically update an accessible official-language citizen guide to RTI covering objects of the Act, CPIO/SPIO contact directory, application process, appeal remedies, Section 4 disclosures, and fee notices.
checkpoints.citation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 26(2), Section 26(3)(a)-(i) & Section 26(4)
checkpoints.public_disclosure_indicator: Official-language RTI Citizen Guide PDF/webpage on Union or State nodal RTI portals.
checkpoints.caveats: Applies specifically to Central/State Appropriate Government nodal RTI portals (e.g., rti.gov.in, dopt.gov.in, and State Government RTI / Information Commission / General Administration portals) — NOT every subordinate domain.
checkpoints.agent_inspection_guidance: Nodal Appropriate Government portal publishes an official-language Citizen RTI Guide covering clauses (a)-(i) of Section 26(3). Partial/stale: Guide exists only in English (omitting official language) or is severely outdated (pre-2012 rules / dead addresses).
